title: When the Cup Becomes a Chain: Drunk in Bondage

sense.text:
“whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning,” The Lord preserved the experiences of the forefathers so we could study them, learn deeply and apply what they show about our own lives. Searching, studying and applying the scriptures is how the learning becomes useful.

The comfort that produces hope is the comfort of the scriptures. Many seek comfort in everything else. There is the comfort Esau offers and the comfort God gives; they are not the same. Gossip, murmuring, fornication and drunkenness can remain where the word is heard but not applied. Do not prefer classes that expose someone else while avoiding the instruction that requires personal accountability.

Drunkenness is not only the picture of a person blacking out. A repeated pattern around alcohol calls for honest self-examination. Evaluate the habit rather than use the absence of the most extreme symptom to excuse it.

precepts.why: “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life:” Christ directs the search toward the scriptures. That returns to Paul's point that what was written is for our learning. Peace, comfort and the way to overcome infirmities must be sought there. Learning requires the effort to search and study, followed by application, rather than finding another means of avoiding the issue.

sense.text:
God is “the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort;” The source of comfort is the heavenly Father, approached through searching the scriptures and seeing our own struggles in the experiences of the forefathers.

The low attention given to classes on alcohol, compared with the excitement over a public debate or someone being cut by the scriptures, exposes an appetite for escape. It is easier to watch another person corrected than to face a problem in oneself. The same avoidance appears when instruction about fornication or another personal sin is passed over without being heard. Comfort from God must be joined to willingness to accept the correction that reveals the problem.

precepts.why:
“Let, I pray thee, thy merciful kindness be for my comfort, according to thy word unto thy servant.” God's merciful kindness provides comfort because he has given time and grace to repent. There remains an opportunity to be made right and delivered from captivity. That opportunity should encourage us rather than make us complacent.

“for thy law is my delight.” The laws of God must be our delight in these last days. The wars, rumours of wars and the awakening of Israelites in places such as Fiji and Bougainville show the urgency of the time. Do not answer that work with continued drunkenness, lying, stealing, envy or hatred within marriage and the body. People sharing the same low condition in captivity should not be consumed with hatred for one another.

sense.text:
“Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.” Mourning should lead to God's comfort, not to dependence on beer, mixed drinks or strong drink. Alcohol can be used to mask something beneath the surface: pain, trouble or feelings a person does not want to face. When the bottle becomes the required source of comfort, the scriptures no longer seem sufficient without drinking alongside them.

Ask what the alcohol is being used to cover. The issue is deeper than whether a drink is present. The habit can also work against care of the body; persistent failure to lose weight is challenged as a reason to examine hidden drinking instead of offering explanations that avoid it. The concern includes the hidden visceral fat around the liver, heart and kidneys, not only the weight visible on the outside. The cup becomes a chain when comfort cannot be imagined without it.

The learning is for us, the Israelites, and patience with scriptural comfort gives hope. God's law, mercy, grace and the chance to get right are the comfort being offered. Seeking drunkenness because one's troubles seem unique abandons that hope.

Alcohol can expose unresolved pain in crying calls, resentment, anger or exaggerated admiration that the person later does not remember. Those patterns should provoke reassessment. The answer is not to insist that no one else could understand, but to recognize the shared struggle of the brethren and keep fighting.

precepts.why:
“There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man:” You are not the only one facing that sin, trial or trauma. Some have already faced it and overcome, some continue fighting, and some have given in and begun making excuses. Knowing that brothers and sisters fight the same fight is a reason to stand with them.

Loss, rejection and earlier harm must not become permission to return to the old life. Find comfort in the scriptures, prove yourself to the Lord and be an example to the brethren. Recognizing that the struggle is shared answers the claim that the bottle is the only relief available.

sense.text:
“Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise.” Alcohol is deceptive. A person may feel little while sitting and then discover the loss of balance upon standing. Strong drink can also bring out rage, making someone ready to fight everyone or imagine a strength he does not have. Being deceived by it is not wisdom.

Evaluate the stages of the habit honestly. The early pattern can begin with social drinking that becomes relief for stress, sleep or anxiety. Tolerance increases, a stressful day becomes a reason one deserves a bottle, and thoughts increasingly return to alcohol as a way to cope, even while the person still appears normal.

The next signs include blackouts, loss of control after intending to have only one drink, drinking secretly, hiding bottles or lying about intake, and drinking before events to feel able to participate. Liquid courage can become a substitute for sober confidence. Shame afterward does not by itself change the pattern.

As dependence takes hold physically and psychologically, the mind becomes occupied with the next buzz. Drinking begins earlier in the day, work is missed, excuses multiply and attempts to stop fail. Responsibilities lose priority. That includes spiritual duties: drinking becomes the reason not to fast, pray, read or attend to the scriptures. The Bible is treated as a buzz kill because the desired comfort has shifted elsewhere.

In the later pattern, a person drinks to function rather than merely to get drunk. Morning shaking, drinking throughout the day, neglect of hygiene and nutrition, and loss of interest in family, classes, camp or other responsibilities show how much has been surrendered to the habit. Coming to the Sabbath gathering still smelling strongly of drink is not excused by saying it was consumed the night before. Being able to speak or walk does not prove freedom from dependence.

Alcoholism is described as a chronic, progressive and potentially fatal disorder marked by excessive or compulsive use and psychological and physical dependence. Harm includes impaired work and relationships, violent behaviour, neglect and alcohol poisoning, as well as consequences such as liver disease and drunk driving. Confidence that one can drive does not remove impairment or its consequences.

A chain confines and restrains. When a person cannot separate himself from the cup, that describes the hold the habit has acquired. The point is self-evaluation, including for men in leadership, rather than defending the bottle. Drinking itself is not being called a sin; excess, drunkenness and a dependence used to escape unresolved troubles are the issue.

Moses addressed Israel coming out of Egypt and warned that failure to hear God's voice and do his commandments would bring curses that overtook the people. To overtake is to conquer: these are conditions the nation struggles against rather than simply choosing to declare itself free of them. Study this foundation instead of assuming that everyone already understands the history.

The Christian claim that the people are not under the curse is challenged by their continuing condition and by worship of a white god. The attachment to a white Jesus is described as a fantasy and fetish, reinforced by stories in which the desired prince is white. Praying to that image for salvation, work or a better marriage leaves the mind looking to the white man even while dismissing the significance of Christ being black.

“Therefore shalt thou serve thine enemies” The enemies named are the white man, the Asian man, the Arab man, the China man and the yellow man. Israel's hunger, thirst, nakedness, want and iron yoke are connected to the captivity of blacks, Hispanics and Native American Indians, with continuing oppression in places including Sudan, Congo and Libya. Prayer without willingness to go and help is contrasted with the prophets' work among the people.

The literal chains have also become mental chains: drugs, despair, alcohol, hatred, envy, loss of identity and lack of purpose. Breaking the mind can hold a person long after a physical wound heals. A person may believe himself free while still serving the power that shaped those beliefs and dependencies.

The causes examined include family history, drinking from an early age, mental-health difficulties, stressful surroundings, alcohol taken with medication, peer pressure, frequent consumption over time, abuse and trauma, and lack of family supervision or support. What matters is how the person feels before reaching for the drink. Pain is temporarily covered, leaving the underlying problem in place.

Entering the truth must not simply replace marijuana or other drugs with liquor. A congregation where drinking is treated like a club can encourage that substitution. The fact that drinking is permitted does not make it a cure for the experiences a person brought with him. Examine the fear, sorrow or abandonment being covered, rather than exchanging one crutch for another.

precepts.why: “Thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will bring evil upon this place, and upon the inhabitants thereof, even all the curses that are written in the book which they have read before the king of Judah:” The curses are evil brought upon the place and its inhabitants, as written in the book read before the king of Judah. This establishes what the curses in Deuteronomy mean: real calamities upon the people, not an abstract label that can be dismissed while their effects continue.

sense.text: “Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, and wine unto those that be of heavy hearts.” The heavy heart explains why many turn to alcohol: they want relief from what they have endured. The issue must be addressed rather than overlooked. Scripture can be supplied continually, but each person still has to take account of what he is doing and why.

“Let him drink, and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more.” Forgetting is the attraction. Poverty, trauma and misery are temporarily pushed out of view, but the cause remains. The question is why that escape is needed and what fear or sorrow lies beneath it.

The report about Whiteclay, Nebraska, describes a town of twenty-two people with four liquor stores beside the dry Pine Ridge reservation. It presents estimates of alcoholism reaching eighty percent and alcohol linked to nearly all of roughly thirteen thousand recorded crimes in the period discussed. The contrast shows others profiting from a people's unresolved affliction.

Loss of land, the killing of chiefs, violence against women and the breaking of the nation leave wounds that drink cannot repair. The nations make money as the people drink to forget. Drunkenness can make the oppressed imitate the white man as robber, murderer and rapist, reproducing harm instead of overcoming it. Seek the comfort of God and address the trouble rather than accept this cycle as the only answer.

“The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth.” The wise face the painful matter and deal with it. The fool seeks the house of mirth to escape what must be addressed. Knowing that there is an issue but insisting on feeling happy instead can turn drinking into a means of hiding from the work of repair. The choice is whether to confront the problem or keep covering it.

Woe, sorrow, contentions, babbling, wounds without cause and red eyes belong to those who linger at wine and seek mixed wine. They are not isolated accidents unrelated to the habit. Sorrow can come out when a certain song plays, then turn into self-pity, arguments or senseless speech. The signs should be recognized as the attributes of drunkenness rather than excused separately each time.

The attraction of the colour in the cup conceals the end: “it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder.” The pleasing appearance does not show what the drink will do when a person remains with it.
Alcohol lowers restraint so that the eyes turn toward strange women and the heart speaks perverse things. What began as seeking relief can become another offence against the commandments.

Lying in the midst of the sea or upon the top of a mast pictures the loss of steadiness. The mast is high on the ship, where the movement is felt strongly. The stumbling person who calls himself merely tipsy is swaying as though upon a moving ship. Claiming not to be drunk does not change the condition being displayed.

precepts.why:
At Darius' feast, three young men of the king's guard offered sentences to be judged for wisdom and reward. The first wrote, “Wine is the strongest.” His argument shows how powerfully wine can overcome distinctions of age, wealth and rank. The king, fatherless child, bondman, freeman, poor and rich can all have their judgment brought to the same condition.

It turns thoughts to jollity so a man remembers neither sorrow nor debt, returning to the forgetting described in Proverbs 31. The relief can make someone feel rich and free from obligation even while the actual poverty remains. It also removes regard for king or governor and leads to uncontrolled speech.

Men in their cups forget love for friends and brethren and draw swords against one another. Companions who came together can end up fighting; the same loss of restraint appears in domestic violence when a drunken man beats his wife. Afterward they may not remember what they did. This explains the sorrow, contention and babbling in Proverbs: overconsumption brings error, damages love and leaves consequences that forgotten memories cannot undo.

sense.text:
“Wine is as good as life to a man, if it be drunk moderately: what life is then to a man that is without wine? for it was made to make men glad.” The permission is joined to moderation. Drinking is not itself being called a sin, but the word moderately cannot be reduced to a feeling that one is not yet drunk. Moderation includes avoiding extremes, observing reasonable limits and remaining temperate.

Look at the pattern as well as the immediate sensation. Not passing out does not prove that alcohol has not become a dependency. Regularly needing it, arranging life around it or defending the pattern when questioned should lead to reassessment. The instruction from Deacon Yosua to evaluate oneself when a pattern appears applies to leaders too.

Dependence can damage both body and mind. Anxiety, depression and suicidal feelings are discussed alongside harm to marriage, family, friendships, work and finances. Those consequences can in turn increase anxiety and the urge to drink again. Drinking to improve the mood can therefore become a vicious cycle rather than a solution. The measure must be the whole course of conduct, not the claim that one still functions.

“Love thine own soul, and comfort thy heart, remove sorrow far from thee: for sorrow hath killed many, and there is no profit therein.” Love of one's own soul is not supplied by alcohol. The heart needs comfort and sorrow must be addressed, rather than allowing the effort to escape it to become another captivity. Drinking can make a person a slave to the bottle while the heaviness remains.

People turn toward alcohol, adultery, fornication, drugs, doubt or withdrawal from God in trying to remove sorrow. Those responses deepen the problem. Do not refuse to bring a burden to leadership because of fear of troubling the body. Avoiding counsel that way is like knowing about cancer but refusing to bring it to a doctor. The work of helping, counselling and taking people through the scriptures exists for those needs.

precepts.why: “For of heaviness cometh death, and the heaviness of the heart breaketh strength.” Heaviness can break a person's strength and bring death. This reinforces the need to deal with sorrow rather than leave it hidden under a coping habit. Concealing the trouble does not remove its weight, and the person should not avoid the help offered through the body.

sense.text:
“Wine measurably drunk and in season bringeth gladness of the heart, and cheerfulness of the mind:” Both measure and season matter. Drinking every day is challenged as not being in season. The pattern is visible to the people closest to a man even when he denies it. A wife may see the daily drinking or find bottles in the car long before he admits what is happening.

Defensiveness does not refute what she sees. Examine the evidence honestly instead of silencing her or pretending the pattern is invisible. That self-examination belongs to leaders too: receive Deacon Yosua's instruction, take a step back and reevaluate the habit instead of treating correction as something for everyone else. Mutual accountability is proposed so the brothers can address dependency and remain blameless.

“But wine drunken with excess maketh bitterness of the mind, with brawling and quarrelling.” Excess can bring back old attachments and painful memories, turning the mind bitter instead of cheerful. The quarrels and brawling are part of that effect. A person may recognize that a particular drink repeatedly brings out old relationships, military experiences or other trauma, yet keep returning to it.

Drunkenness increases a fool's rage until he offends. Words that would not be spoken sober can become insults and disrespect. The drunk declaration, I always hated your ass, nigga, exposes a hostility that has been kept hidden. It wounds relationships as well as putting the body in danger.

“it diminisheth strength, and maketh wounds.” Waking with injuries or evidence of events one cannot remember is no sign of strength. The comic extremes in The Hangover illustrate the loss of control, but the underlying issue is the real damage caused when a person has surrendered judgment and restraint.

“Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:” Vigilance depends on sobriety. Satan seeks someone to devour, and the danger is also applied to a white enemy waiting for an opportunity while the man is impaired. A household left with its protector drunk, blacked out or unable to see clearly is exposed when trouble comes.

The coming conditions require readiness. Drunkenness and vigilance cannot coexist, any more than confidence after drinking makes a driver alert and safe. The same warning applies to careless drinking with worldly companions and assuming that familiarity guarantees safety. Do not be caught slipping when the need to act arrives.

precepts.why:
Sound doctrine requires aged men to be sober, grave and temperate, sound in faith, charity and patience. Sobriety is part of the character needed for those responsibilities. A man cannot cultivate that maturity while using alcohol to keep avoiding the issues before him.

Men and women must face the problems rather than try to make them disappear under drink. Unaddressed trauma, stress or abandonment continue to obstruct spiritual growth. The reasons given for drinking can themselves reveal where faith and the work of overcoming are needed. Scripture's repeated attention to alcohol is a reason to take the matter seriously.

sense.text:
“I sought the Lord, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears.” The fears are connected to the reasons offered for excessive drinking and the feeling that one cannot stop. Seek the Lord about the underlying fear, trauma and sorrow, not only the outward habit used to cover them. The work has to go beneath the surface.

Drinking itself is not being condemned. Overconsumption, drunkenness and using liquor as a crutch are the issue. Answering concern about alcoholism with a remark about Christ making wine evades the problem. If alcohol is masking a feeling or wound, that burden needs to be addressed instead of defended as a reason the pattern must continue.

precepts.why: “hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God.” The cast-down and disquieted soul is directed toward hope and praise. God is the help to seek when the inward condition is troubled. This joins the search for deliverance from fear to the source of comfort, rather than making the bottle the answer to a downcast spirit.

sense.text:
“And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind,” The world being resisted is the white man's world and its normalized drinking culture. A new man or woman requires a renewed mind rather than simply copying what the surroundings encourage.

An alcohol-promoting environment makes drinking ordinary, accessible, affordable and desirable through marketing and social pressure. Alcohol is presented as fun, and even machines that mix drinks at home remove the need to go to a bar. These are features of the American culture around the people. Their prevalence does not make them the pattern God's people should follow.

“And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares.” The day is the day of destruction. Surfeiting, drunkenness and the cares of this life can overcharge the heart so that it arrives unawares. Alcohol takes away perception and judgment, including a sense of time and what is happening around the person. Self-watchfulness is necessary if the people are to be ready rather than distracted and impaired when the day comes.

“The righteous cry, and the Lord heareth, and delivereth them out of all their troubles.” Bring the pain, woes and trauma to the Lord. Cry to him, repent, turn from sin and apply what is learned. The answer is not to call for more liquor while hiding the problem. Study, prayer and accountability belong to honest self-examination.

Ask whether alcohol is consuming too much of life and whether it is being concealed. Admitting a problem makes it possible to address it together instead of pretending not to see what is already known. Men and women of the Lord must face those matters if their minds are to be ready for what is coming.

The proposed commitment among the brothers is to take time away from drinking and hold one another accountable. A month, two months or three months away, or restricting drink to an actual season rather than a daily pattern, is offered as an opportunity for self-examination. The inability to keep a chosen limit exposes the dependency that needs attention. Hiding liquor is also a reason to stop denying the issue and seek that shared help.

The vanishing world reaches its end and the books are opened before the firmament for all to see. The warnings concern the finish of the present order, giving urgency to preparing the mind and overcoming what holds it captive.
Friends fight like enemies and the earth stands in fear. This is the destruction for which the people must be ready, not a time to surrender awareness to alcohol.

Those who remain through the things foretold escape and see God's salvation and the end of the wicked world. Men received without having tasted death see it, and the inhabitants' hearts are changed and turned to another meaning. The change belongs to the deliverance being awaited.

“For evil shall be put out, and deceit shall be quenched.” Faith flourishes and corruption is overcome. The application includes alcoholism, drug addiction, anxiety, depression, mental-health troubles, PTSD and trauma: these forms of corruption will not remain in that day. The truth long without fruit will be declared.

That promised end is a reason to keep fighting now. Do not settle into the chains of the mind or treat the present burden as permanent. Continue the work of overcoming and let go of what binds the soul.

precepts.why: The change is connected to “in the twinkling of an eye,” The inhabitants' changed hearts in 2 Esdras are joined to the change at God's deliverance. The point is the transformation of those received, including those who have not tasted death, at the end of this present world.
